contribution.value: OpenBookQA is a new 5,957-question multiple-choice QA benchmark paired with a 1,326-fact open book of elementary science, requiring multi-hop reasoning that combines a core fact with broad common knowledge.

ev.quote: We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA, modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject. The open book that comes with our questions is a set of 1326 elementary level science facts. Roughly 6000 questions probe an understanding of these facts
The OpenBookQA dataset consists of about 6,000 4-way multiple-choice questions, each associated with one core fact from a "book" F of 1326 such facts

datasets.value: F: 1,326 elementary science facts (open book, subset of WorldTree)

ev.quote: For F, we use a subset of the WorldTree corpus which Jansen et al. (2018) have analyzed for sufficiency for elementary level science. The subset we use is taken from the 2287 WorldTree facts that were marked as "central"

datasets.value: K: ~6,000 auxiliary common-knowledge facts (crowdsourced second facts)

ev.quote: We thus include in OpenBookQA the set K of such second facts only as auxiliary data for optional use. We emphasize that K should not be viewed as 'gold' additional facts
adding ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017) introduces a distraction and reduces the score
When we also include facts retrieved from WordNet (Miller et al., 1990), the score improves by about 0.5%

data_size.value: 5,957 multiple-choice questions split 4,957/500/500 for Train/Dev/Test; 1,326 core science facts; ~6,000 auxiliary K facts

ev.quote: OpenBookQA consists of 5957 questions, with 4957/500/500 in the Train/Dev/Test splits.
PMI (Clark et al., 2016) uses pointwise mutual information (PMI) to score each answer choice using statistics based on a corpus of 280 GB of plain text
TableILP (Khashabi et al., 2016) is an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) based reasoning system designed for science questions
TupleInference (Khot et al., 2017), also an ILP-based QA system, uses Open IE tuples (Banko et al., 2007) as its semi-structured representation
DGEM (Khot et al., 2018) is a neural entailment model that also uses Open IE to produce a semi-structured representation

ev.section: 4.2 No Training; F and Extr. Knowledge
ev.quote: We also consider providing the set F of core facts to two existing solvers: the IR solver of Clark et al. (2016)

models_used.value: Embeddings + Similarities (logistic regression with GloVe centroids)

ev.quote: We first experiment with a simple logistic regression model (Mihaylov and Nakov, 2016; Mihaylov and Frank, 2016, 2017) that uses centroid vectors r_s^{emb} of the word embeddings
We also experiment with a model where r_q^{ctx} and r_{c_i}^{ctx} are obtained using token-wise interaction proposed in ESIM (Chen et al., 2017b)
(a) Plausible Answer Detector. This baseline goes to the extreme of completely ignoring q and trying to learn how plausible it is for c_i to be the correct answer
(b) Odd-One-Out Solver. It considers all 4 answer options jointly and selects the one that is least similar to the others
(c) Question Match. This solver tries to predict which choice best matches the question (Nakov et al., 2016), without relying on external knowledge

models_used.value: Knowledge-Enhanced Reader (variant of Mihaylov and Frank, 2018)

ev.quote: Knowledge-Enhanced Reader. As a base knowledge-aware model, we use a variant of the model of Mihaylov and Frank (2018), implemented by extending our BiLSTM max-out question-match baseline (c)

models_used.value: ELMo (Peters et al., 2018) - applied to Question Match and ESIM

ev.quote: For Question Match and ESIM we also experiment with ElMo (Peters et al., 2018) which improved their score on Test with 0.4% and 1.8%

models_used.value: GloVe 300d embeddings (840B Common Crawl tokens) - input embeddings

ev.quote: For all experiments we use d = 300 GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) embeddings pre-trained on 840B tokens from Common Crawl

eval_metrics.value: accuracy (% correct on 4-way multiple choice; tie credit 1/k)

ev.quote: For each question, a solver receives 1 point towards this score if it chooses the correct answer, and 1/k if it reports a k-way tie that includes the correct answer
Scores obtained by various solvers on Open-BookQA, reported as a percentage ± the standard deviation across 5 runs with different random seeds

key_results.value: Human performance on OpenBookQA Test = 91.7% (Dev = 89.3%); reported as conservative Ĥ(Q)-3% lower estimate

ev.quote: Human solver | 89.3* | 91.7*

key_results.value: Best knowledge-free trained baseline (Question Match / Odd-one-out) reaches 50.2% Test accuracy, far below the ~92% human level
Pre-trained science QA solvers perform near random: TupleInference 17.9%, PMI 21.2%, TableILP 23.4%, DGEM 24.4% on Test

ev.quote: TupleInference | 15.9 | 17.9

key_results.value: Oracle Knowledge-Enhanced Reader given gold f and k reaches 76.9% Test, still ~15 points below human performance

ev.quote: We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA, modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of a subject
We present a new kind of question answering dataset, OpenBookQA

strengths.value: Introduces a novel open-book QA paradigm forcing multi-hop reasoning that joins one provided science fact with external common knowledge.

ev.section: Question: ... Heat travels through a thermal conductor.
ev.quote: OpenBookQA questions are challenging as they require multi-hop reasoning with partial context provided by F

strengths.value: Multi-stage crowdsourcing plus IR/word-association adversarial filtering yields questions that defeat retrieval-only baselines.

ev.quote: verifies that (a) neither of them answers q_{mc} correctly and (b) the top 3 IR retrieved sentences are insufficient to answer q_{mc}

strengths.value: Reports a principled human-performance estimate (~92%) using Hoeffding's inequality with high-confidence lower bounds.

ev.quote: H˜ (Q) − 3% with probability over 98.8% and at least H˜ (Q) − 2.5% with prob 95.6%; we report the former as our conservative estimate on human performance

strengths.value: Includes ablations with simplistic baselines (Plausible Answer Detector, Odd-One-Out) that expose human bias artifacts in crowdsourced QA data.

ev.quote: the "plausible answer detector" can predict the correct answer with 49.6% accuracy without even looking at the question

weaknesses.value: Auxiliary fact set K is acknowledged as noisy: "often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related" to the question.

ev.quote: These second facts, unfortunately, were often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to q

weaknesses.value: 21% of crowdsourced questions did not actually require the seed science fact, exposing a residual single-hop shortcut.

ev.quote: In 21% of the cases, the crowdsourced question actually tests for a fact that doesn't necessarily need the original science fact

weaknesses.value: Independence assumption for human-accuracy bound is acknowledged as imperfect because the same worker may answer multiple questions.

ev.quote: Realistically, there is some dependence across questions as a single worker may answer multiple questions. We leave a formal analysis of this setting as future work

weaknesses.value: Adding ConceptNet to the knowledge-enhanced reader hurts accuracy, indicating brittle knowledge-retrieval rather than robust reasoning.

ev.quote: adding ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017) introduces a distraction and reduces the score

limitations.value: Restricted to elementary-level science multiple-choice questions; does not test free-form generation, dialogue, or multilingual settings.

ev.quote: The OpenBookQA dataset consists of about 6,000 4-way multiple-choice questions

limitations.value: Open book F (1,326 facts) is small and curated; method does not scale-test retrieval over web-scale or noisy corpora.

ev.quote: we use a subset of the WorldTree corpus ... We further filter them down to 1326 that appear general enough to be applicable to multiple situations

limitations.value: Best system needs gold oracle facts (f and k) to reach 76.9%; realistic retrieval is left as an open challenge.

ev.quote: improved knowledge retrieval should help on this task. At the same time, we are still not close to the human performance level of 92%

limitations.value: No evaluation on instruction-tuned LLMs, transformer-based models, or modern pre-trained language models (paper predates BERT-era systems).

ev.quote: Bold denotes the best Test score in each category.

future_work_stated.value: Solve the multi-hop knowledge-retrieval problem and close the large gap to human performance.

ev.quote: We leave it as a challenge to solve the retrieval problem in this multi-hop setting and to close the large gap to human performance

future_work_stated.value: Use the gold fact f provided in Train/Dev as intermediate supervision (partial explanation) for q.

ev.quote: We leave closing this gap for future research, and illustrate, via oracle-style experiments, the potential of better retrieval and reasoning on this task
